facts.title: Named After a Color
facts.text: The word arsenic traces back to the Greek 'arsenikon', which itself came from the Syriac 'zarniqa' and ultimately the Old Iranian word for gold, referring to the brilliant golden-yellow mineral orpiment (arsenic sulfide). Ancient writers used the term for the colorful sulfide minerals long before the pure element was isolated. The Greek root was sometimes mistakenly linked to 'arsenikos', meaning masculine or potent, reflecting old beliefs about the substance's strength.

facts.title: Isolated by Albertus Magnus
facts.text: Although arsenic compounds were known and used for thousands of years, the medieval scholar Albertus Magnus is usually credited with first isolating the element around 1250 by heating orpiment with soap. This makes arsenic one of the very first elements to be isolated in a recognizable elemental form, centuries before modern chemistry existed. Earlier alchemists in the Islamic world, including Jabir ibn Hayyan, had already studied its compounds extensively.

facts.title: It Skips the Liquid Phase
facts.text: At ordinary atmospheric pressure, gray arsenic does not melt into a liquid when heated; instead it sublimates, turning directly from a solid into a vapor at about 615 degrees Celsius. To get liquid arsenic you must heat it under pressure of roughly 28 atmospheres or more. This unusual behavior set it apart from most metals and made it tricky for early chemists to purify.

facts.title: Three Faces of One Element
facts.text: Arsenic exists in several allotropes, the most common being a brittle, metallic gray form, alongside a yellow waxy form and a black amorphous form. Gray arsenic has a layered crystal structure similar to that of black phosphorus and conducts electricity, while yellow arsenic is soft, unstable, and made of tetrahedral As4 molecules much like white phosphorus. Exposure to light or gentle heat quickly converts the unstable yellow form back into the stable gray one.

facts.title: A Metalloid on the Staircase
facts.text: Arsenic sits along the zig-zag dividing line of the periodic table that separates metals from nonmetals, which is why it is classified as a metalloid with properties of both. It shares group 15 with nitrogen and phosphorus above it and with antimony and bismuth below, so it shows the typical valences of plus three and plus five. This in-between character is exactly why arsenic is so valuable in making semiconductors.

facts.title: The Heart of Gallium Arsenide
facts.text: Combined with gallium, arsenic forms gallium arsenide, a semiconductor that moves electrons faster than silicon and converts electricity into light very efficiently. This compound powers high-frequency chips in mobile phones and radar, the red and infrared LEDs in remote controls, and high-efficiency solar cells used on satellites and Mars rovers. Without arsenic, much of modern high-speed and optoelectronic technology would look very different.

facts.title: From Poison to Pharmacy
facts.text: In 1910 Paul Ehrlich and his team introduced Salvarsan, an arsenic-based drug that became the first effective treatment for syphilis and a founding example of modern chemotherapy. More recently, arsenic trioxide, once feared purely as a poison, has become a highly successful medicine for acute promyelocytic leukemia, often producing remission when other treatments fail. The same element that kills can, in carefully controlled doses, save lives.

facts.title: The Inheritance Powder
facts.text: Arsenic trioxide earned the grim nickname 'inheritance powder' in Renaissance Europe because it is nearly tasteless, dissolves easily in food and drink, and once produced symptoms resembling natural illness. For centuries it was almost untraceable, until chemist James Marsh devised the sensitive Marsh test in 1836, which could reveal tiny amounts of arsenic in a body. That breakthrough turned forensic toxicology into a real science and made arsenic poisoning far easier to detect.

facts.title: A Hidden Threat in Groundwater
facts.text: Naturally occurring arsenic leaches from certain rocks and sediments into groundwater, and in regions of Bangladesh and West Bengal millions of people have been exposed by drinking from contaminated wells. The World Health Organization sets a safety limit of just 10 micrograms of arsenic per liter of drinking water. This contamination is considered one of the largest mass poisonings in human history, driving major efforts in well testing and filtration.

facts.title: Life That Tolerates Arsenic
facts.text: Although arsenic is toxic to most organisms because it mimics phosphorus and disrupts energy metabolism, some microbes have evolved to thrive around it. Certain bacteria can actually use arsenic compounds in their metabolism, breathing arsenate the way we breathe oxygen, in environments like California's Mono Lake. Studying these extremophiles helps scientists understand the chemical limits of life and even how life might survive on other worlds.
